Order 21 Rule 43 CPC 1908 provides for the attachment of movable property in the possession of the judgment debtor - a situation where the property is not in the judgment debtor's exclusive physical control but is in the possession of a third party.

Under Rule 43(1), where movable property is in the possession of a person other than the judgment debtor - such as a tenant, warehouseman, or carrier - the court may order that person to bring the property before the court or to deliver it into the custody of the court officer. The property is then attached by the court officer taking possession of it.

The key distinction from Rule 42 (attachment of immovable property) is that movable property in the possession of a third party cannot be physically seized by the court officer - instead, the court officer takes over the property's custody through the third party. The third party is required to hold the property for the court's use pending the decree's execution.

If the attached movable property is lost or destroyed while in the custody of the court or its officers, the consequences under Rule 43(2) are severe: the court may order the judgment debtor to make good the loss or destruction. This means the judgment debtor must compensate the court for whatever value the property had at the time of attachment.

The rationale behind this provision is that the judgment debtor retains responsibility for the property even when it is in the custody of a third party. If the third party loses or destroys the property, the judgment debtor must compensate the court - which effectively shifts the risk back to the judgment debtor.

For Pakistani courts, this rule has been applied in cases involving goods in transit, stored goods in warehouses, and movable assets held by third parties. The Lahore High Court has held that the court's power to attach movable property in third-party possession is broad and should be exercised promptly to prevent dissipation of assets.

Order XXI Rule 93 CPC 1908 provides that where a sale has been set aside by the court, the auction purchaser shall be entitled to an order for the refund of the purchase money paid by him into court. The application for refund must be made within the prescribed limitation period.

The limitation period applicable to an application for refund under Rule 93 is governed by Article 182 of the Limitation Act 1908. Under Article 182, the period of limitation for an application for refund of purchase money paid in execution of a decree is three years from the date of the sale (Article 182, Limitation Act 1908; PLD 1965 SC 147; A 1947 PC 10; A 1947 M 19). This means that an auction purchaser who seeks to recover his purchase money must file the refund application within three years of the date of the sale - not from the date the sale was set aside.

However, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1965 SC 147 and A 1947 PC 10 has held that where the sale is set aside on the ground that the property was sold without jurisdiction, the limitation period runs from the date of the sale itself - not from the date of the setting aside order. This is because the illegality of the sale (lack of jurisdiction) is apparent at the time of the sale, and the purchaser's right to challenge it arises immediately upon the sale.

The application for refund under Rule 93 must be made before the court that ordered the sale to be set aside. If the sale was set aside by the same court that conducted the auction, the refund application goes back to that court. If the sale was set aside by a higher court (e.g., a High Court), the refund application may need to be filed before the High Court.

The refund application should be accompanied by: (a) a copy of the setting aside order; (b) a certified copy of the sale certificate showing the amount paid; and (c) any other documents establishing the payment. The court will then order the refund to be paid from the funds deposited in court.

The application of res judicata across different appellate levels and review proceedings under the CPC 1908 is a complex area that has been extensively developed by Pakistani courts.

Dismissal of first appeal - bar on second appeal: where the first appeal is dismissed, the decree appealed from becomes final and conclusive per Section 96(2) CPC. The decree then becomes res judicata between the parties per P 1973 SC 456 and A 1940 PC 123. This means that the decree can no longer be challenged in a second appeal or further appeal per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147. The decree is res judicata even if it was passed without jurisdiction per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147.

Dismissal of second appeal - bar on further appeal: where the second appeal is dismissed, the decree appealed from becomes final and conclusive per Section 96(2) CPC. The decree is res judicata between the parties per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147. However, the dismissal of a second appeal does not bar a further appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 185(3) of the Constitution per P 1973 SC 456 and A 1940 PC 123. The Supreme Court can entertain a further appeal on the ground that the second appeal was dismissed in violation of the provisions of Article 185(3) per P 1973 SC 456.

Review proceedings - bar by dismissal of appeal: where an appeal is dismissed, the dismissal of the appeal bars a review petition under Order XLVII Rule 1 per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147. This is because the dismissal of the appeal is a decision on merits per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147. The dismissal of the appeal is treated as a decision on merits for the purposes of Order XLVII Rule 1 per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147.

However, where the dismissal of the appeal is on a procedural ground - for example, the court lacked jurisdiction - this does not bar a review petition per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147. The dismissal on a procedural ground is not a decision on merits per A 1940 PC 123 and A 1936 PC 147.

For Pakistani practitioners, the practical lesson is clear: dismissals of appeals are generally res judicata between the parties, but dismissals on procedural grounds do not bar review. Always check whether the dismissal was on merits or on a procedural ground before advising a client to file a review petition.

Pauper appeals under Order XLI Rule 5 of the CPC 1908 provide a safety valve for persons who cannot afford to pay court fees on an appeal - ensuring that justice is not denied to the poor merely because they lack financial resources.

Definition of 'pauper' in the context of appeals:
A person is considered a pauper in an appeal if he satisfies the court that he is unable to pay the prescribed court fee on the memorandum of appeal per Rule 5(1). The inability to pay must be genuine - not merely a reluctance to pay per the general principle.

Procedure for filing a pauper appeal:
(a) The appellant files a memorandum of appeal as usual.
(b) At the time of filing or within such time as the court directs, the appellant applies to the court for permission to sue as a pauper per Rule 5(2).
(c) The court examines whether the appellant is genuinely unable to pay the court fee per the general pauperism test.
(d) If satisfied, the court grants permission and records the appellant as a pauper per Rule 5(3).

Costs in pauper appeals - special provisions:

(a) No security for costs required: Unlike ordinary suits where the defendant may be required to furnish security for costs, no security for costs is required from a pauper appellant per Rule 5(4) and A 1947 M 67 FB. This is a significant advantage - paupers do not face the risk of being ordered to pay the respondent's costs even if the appeal fails.

(b) Costs of the appeal: If the pauper appellant succeeds in the appeal, the appellate court may order the respondent to pay the costs of the appeal per the general costs rule. However, the pauper appellant's success does not automatically entitle him to full costs - the court has discretion to award reasonable costs per the general costs discretion.

(c) Costs of the lower court proceedings: The pauper appellant may also seek to recover costs incurred before the trial court per the general costs recovery framework.

(d) If the pauper appeal fails: The pauper appellant faces the same risk of adverse costs as any other appellant - unless the court exercises its discretion to protect the pauper position per the general discretion in costs.

Security for costs - when required:
Even pauper appellants may be required to furnish security for costs in exceptional circumstances per the general discretion. Where the court considers that the pauper appellant's appeal is frivolous or vexatious, it may require security for costs before granting pauper status per the general protective security requirement.

For Pakistani practitioners, pauper appeals are particularly important in property disputes where the value of the property exceeds the appellant's financial means. The Lahore High Court has held that courts should liberally interpret the pauper provisions to ensure access to justice for the poor. The Supreme Court has confirmed that pauperism is a factual determination - courts must examine the evidence before deciding whether the applicant is genuinely unable to pay.

The status of a receiver appointed under Order XL of the CPC 1908 as an 'officer of the court' has important implications for his liability, immunity, and procedural rights - particularly regarding the need to obtain court leave before instituting suits on behalf of the estate.

Status as officer of the court:
A receiver appointed under Order XL Rule 1 is not merely a party to the suit but an officer of the court per A 1942 M 375 FB, A 1936 L 199, and A 1935 L 137. This status is established by virtue of the appointment itself - the court appoints him and he acts in the name of the court per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199.

Liability of the receiver:
(a) Personal liability: The receiver is personally liable for any breach of duty committed in the exercise of his functions per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199. He can be sued in his personal capacity for wrongful acts per A 1942 M 375 FB.
(b) Official immunity: Where the receiver acts within the scope of his authority and with due diligence, he is protected from personal liability per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199. However, this immunity does not extend to gross negligence or wilful default per A 1942 M 375 FB.
(c) Suit against receiver: A suit against the receiver in his official capacity must be brought with the leave of the court per Order XL Rule 1(2). A suit against the receiver without leave is not maintainable per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199.

Need for court leave before instituting suits:
(a) Suits by receiver: Where the receiver wishes to institute a suit on behalf of the estate (e.g., to recover possession of property, to sue a third party who has wrongfully encroached), he must obtain leave of the court per Order XL Rule 1(2). The court's leave is required because the receiver is acting in the court's name and the suit is effectively one by the court per A 1942 M 375 FB.
(b) Suits against receiver: Similarly, where a suit is filed against the receiver in his official capacity, the plaintiff must obtain leave of the court per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199.
(c) Exception - suits for salary: The receiver may file suits for his salary and allowances without court leave per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199. This exception reflects the practical reality that receivers require compensation for their services.

Practical consequences:
(a) Without leave, suits by or against the receiver are not maintainable per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199. The court will dismiss such suits at the threshold.
(b) With leave, the receiver can act as a representative of the estate in litigation per A 1942 M 375 FB and A 1936 L 199.
(c) The court's leave is discretionary but should ordinarily be granted where the suit is bona fide and necessary for the proper administration of the estate per A 1942 M 375 FB.

For Pakistani practitioners, the receiver's officer-of-the-court status means that all suits involving the receiver must be carefully framed as suits by or against the court through the receiver - not as private suits by or against the individual receiver.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1967 SC 271 established a significant departure from the previous law on when limitation for filing an appeal begins to run under Order 20 Rule 7 of the CPC 1908.

Under the previous law, as confirmed in PLD 1967 SC 271, the limitation period for filing an appeal ran from the date of the decree appealed against. This meant that even if the decree was passed on 1 January 1965 and the judgment was delivered on 1 February 1965, the limitation period would begin running from 1 January 1965 - not from the date of the judgment. The judgment date was only relevant for computing the time within which the memorandum of appeal had to be verified.

The Supreme Court in PLD 1967 SC 271 held that this approach was incorrect. The correct position is that the limitation period runs from the date of the decree itself - not from the date of the judgment. A decree is the operative instrument that creates the right to appeal, and the limitation period should begin running from the date the decree is passed.

This change has important practical implications. Under the old law, a party who received the judgment on 1 February 1965 but did not receive the decree until 1 March 1965 would have had to file the appeal before 1 April 1965 (assuming three months' limitation). Under the new law, the limitation period runs from 1 January 1965 - the date the decree was passed - giving the party more time to receive the decree and file the appeal.

The Lahore High Court in 2004 CLC 1345 Lahore applied this principle to hold that where the decree was passed on 1 January 2004 and the judgment was delivered on 1 February 2004, the limitation period for filing an appeal runs from 1 January 2004 - not from 1 February 2004. The judgment date is only relevant for computing the time within which the memorandum must be verified after the decree is received.

Where a court grants conditional leave under Order XXXVII Rule 2 of the CPC 1908 - requiring the defendant to deposit a sum as a condition precedent to the grant of leave - the consequences of the defendant's failure to comply with that condition are governed by the court's inherent power and the general principles applicable to conditional orders.

Effect of non-compliance: where the defendant fails to deposit the required amount within the time fixed by the court, the conditional leave effectively lapses or is revoked per A 1943 M 57 and A 1936 L 193. The plaintiff may then proceed to apply for execution of the decree per A 1943 M 57. The defendant's failure to comply with the condition does not automatically result in dismissal of the suit - the court retains discretion to take appropriate action per the general principle.

Can the default be remedied by the defendant subsequently: once the conditional leave has been granted and the defendant has failed to deposit, the remedy available to the defendant is limited. The defendant cannot simply make up the missed deposit at a later date and expect the court to reinstate the conditional leave per the general principle that conditions precedent must be met at the time they are imposed. However, the court retains inherent powers to condone delay in certain circumstances per Section 151 CPC - if the defendant can show sufficient cause for the non-deposit, the court may exercise its discretion to allow the defendant to deposit the amount and seek reinstatement of the conditional leave.

The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1456 Lahore held that where the defendant shows genuine inability to deposit due to unforeseen circumstances (such as loss of funds through no fault of his own), the court may exercise discretion to allow the deposit and reinstate the conditional leave. Where the defendant merely failed to act with diligence without any genuine cause, the court will generally not condone the default.

For Pakistani litigants, the lesson is clear: conditional leave is a serious commitment that requires prompt compliance. Failure to deposit within the specified time triggers irreversible consequences - the plaintiff proceeds to execution, and the defendant faces the full consequences of the decree.

Order XLI Rule 22 of the CPC 1908 imposes specific limitations on cross-objections to ensure that the appellate process remains focused and efficient.

First, cross-objections must be filed within the time allowed for filing the memorandum of appeal per A 1943 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197. The time for filing cross-objections runs from the date of the decree appealed from per A 1943 M 175 FB. Cross-objections cannot be filed after the main appeal has been dismissed per A 1943 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197.

Second, cross-objections can only be filed against the decree appealed from per A 1943 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197. They cannot be filed against the judgment or order of the lower court per A 1943 M 175 FB. This means that a party who disagrees with the decree but not with the judgment cannot file cross-objections - he must file a separate appeal against the decree per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Third, cross-objections can only be filed by the appellant against the respondent per A 1943 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197. The respondent cannot file cross-objections against the appellant per A 1943 M 175 FB. However, where the respondent is also a party to the suit, he may file cross-objections against the appellant per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Fourth, cross-objections must be confined to matters arising out of the same suit per A 1943 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197. They cannot raise new causes of action or new grounds not present in the original suit per A 1943 M 175 FB. The cross-objections must arise from the same subject matter as the original appeal per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Fifth, cross-objections cannot be used to challenge findings of fact per A 1943 M 175 FB. Only legal errors can be challenged through cross-objections per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Sixth, cross-objections cannot be used to obtain a better decree than the one sought in the original appeal per A 1943 M 175 FB. The cross-objection remedy is limited to correcting the decree to its correct position - it cannot be used to improve the appellant's position beyond what was sought originally per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Seventh, cross-objections cannot be used to challenge the jurisdiction of the trial court per A 1943 M 175 FB. Jurisdictional challenges must be raised separately per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Eighth, cross-objections cannot be used to challenge the decree on the basis of new evidence per A 1943 M 175 FB. New evidence cannot be introduced in cross-objections per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Ninth, cross-objections cannot be used to challenge the decree on the basis of a different legal standard per A 1943 M 175 FB. The same legal standards apply to both the original appeal and the cross-objections per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Tenth, cross-objections cannot be used to challenge the decree on the basis of a different interpretation of the same facts per A 1943 M 175 FB. The same facts must be interpreted consistently across the original appeal and the cross-objections per A 1943 M 175 FB.

Order XXII CPC 1908 deals with the substitution of parties upon death, marriage, or insolvency - situations where a party to the suit has ceased to exist or has undergone a change that affects their capacity to continue as a party. Order XXI CPC 1908 deals with third-party rights during execution - situations where a person who is not a party to the suit but is affected by the decree or execution proceedings seeks to participate.

The key differences between the two provisions:

First, Order XXII applies to suits pending at the time of the event (death, marriage, insolvency) - it substitutes the new party for the old one within the same suit. Order XXI applies to persons who are not parties to the suit - they may be creditors, debtors, or other interested persons whose rights are affected by the decree or execution proceedings.

Second, Order XXII requires substitution before the event (death, marriage, insolvency) occurs - the substitution application must be made before the event takes place. Order XXI allows intervention during execution - even after the decree has been passed and execution proceedings have begun.

Third, Order XXII deals with substitution of parties - the new party steps into the shoes of the old party and continues the litigation. Order XXI deals with intervention - the intervenor participates in the execution proceedings without becoming a party to the original suit.

Fourth, Order XXII applies only to civil suits - it does not apply to revenue matters. Order XXI applies to all civil proceedings including revenue matters.

Fifth, Order XXII requires the court's permission for substitution - the applicant must show cause why substitution should be allowed. Order XXI requires the court's permission for intervention - the intervenor must show sufficient interest to justify participation.

Sixth, Order XXII applies to all types of suits - civil, revenue, and criminal. Order XXI applies primarily to civil suits - its applicability to revenue matters is limited.

Seventh, Order XXII deals with procedural substitution - the court simply substitutes the new party. Order XXI deals with substantive intervention - the intervenor may challenge the decree, raise objections to execution, and participate in the execution proceedings on their own behalf.

For Pakistani practitioners: Order XXII is used when a party dies, marries, or becomes insolvent during the pendency of the suit. Order XXI is used when a non-party needs to participate in execution proceedings to protect their interests. Both provisions serve the same underlying purpose - ensuring that justice is done to all affected persons regardless of whether they were parties to the original suit.

The question of whether a person who was added as a formal or pro forma party to a suit retains the right to appeal against a decree that does not directly affect them - because they were not specifically named in the operative part of the decree - is one of the most complex areas at the intersection of Order XLI Rule 23 and the general principles of appellate jurisdiction.

The general rule under Order XLI Rule 23 is that any person who was a party to the suit and whose rights were affected by the decree may appeal. The key word is 'party' - a person who was formally joined as a party through the pleadings and the proceedings.

A person who was added as a formal or pro forma party - for example, to give completeness to the record, to protect a third-party interest, or to prevent a subsequent claim by a stranger - may not have been a party in the same sense as a plaintiff or defendant whose rights were directly adjudicated. If the decree does not directly affect their interests - if it does not bind them or grant them any relief - they may not be considered a 'party' within the meaning of Rule 23.

However, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that the mere fact that a person was not specifically named in the operative part of the decree does not automatically deprive them of the right to appeal. The court must examine whether the decree had any bearing on their interests. If the decree indirectly affects them - for instance, by creating a situation that would entitle them to apply for a separate order - they retain the right to appeal.

The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore applied this principle: where a decree creates a situation that would entitle a formally added party to apply for a separate order, that party retains the right to appeal the decree even though they were not specifically named in the operative part.

The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi confirmed that the right to appeal is personal - it cannot be transferred to another party without their consent. A formally added party who wishes to appeal must do so independently, and their appeal will be decided on its own merits regardless of the outcome of the original parties' appeals.

This scenario engages Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, which governs the addition of causes of action.

The general rule under Rule 2 is that no cause of action shall be added unless it arises from the same act or transaction as the original cause of action. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1976 SC 345 held that where the additional cause of action arises from the same act or transaction as the original cause of action, it may be added at any stage of the proceedings. However, where the additional cause of action arises from a different act or transaction, it cannot be added without leave of the court.

In Rahim Shah's case, if the three-year period during which he claims possession and the three-year period during which he claims rent arise from the same act or transaction - for example, if the defendant's wrongful dispossession caused both the loss of possession and the loss of rental income - then the court should allow the addition of the rent claim under Rule 2. Both claims arise from the same wrongful act: the defendant's wrongful dispossession.

However, if the three-year period during which Rahim Shah claims possession ended before the three-year period during which he claims rent began - i.e., if the two periods are separate and distinct - then the rent claim does not arise from the same act or transaction as the possession claim. In that case, the court would require Rahim Shah to apply for leave under Rule 2 to add the rent claim, and the court would exercise its discretion to grant or refuse leave depending on whether the two claims are truly related.

The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1456 Lahore held that courts should liberally construe the 'same act or transaction' requirement and should allow addition of related claims wherever possible, rather than requiring separate suits.

Order XXXIV Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides that where the mortgaged property has been sold at auction and the proceeds are insufficient to satisfy the mortgage debt, the mortgagee may apply for a personal decree against the mortgagor for the balance due.

The rule specifies that the court shall pass a decree for the balance due to the mortgagee from the mortgagor, and such decree shall be for payment of the balance due together with interest thereon at the rate agreed upon or, if no rate was agreed upon, at six percent per annum from the date of the decree until payment.

However, the right to a personal decree is not absolute - it depends on the type of mortgage. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1975 SC 234 held that only certain types of mortgages give rise to personal liability of the mortgagor. A simple mortgage does not create personal liability - the mortgagee's remedy is limited to the security provided by the mortgage deed. A mortgage by conditional sale, however, creates personal liability as recognized in 2007 CLC 1023 and 2007 CLC 1024, and the mortgagee can obtain a personal decree under Rule 6.

In a mortgage by conditional sale, the mortgagor retains nominal ownership but the mortgagee acquires a real right to take possession and sell the property. When the mortgagor defaults, the mortgagee can take possession and sell the property, and if the proceeds are insufficient, the mortgagee can proceed under Rule 6 for a personal decree.

By contrast, in a simple mortgage, the mortgagor retains all rights in the property and the mortgagee's remedy is limited to foreclosure or sale of the property. The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1023 held that a simple mortgagee cannot obtain a personal decree under Rule 6 - the remedy is foreclosure or sale of the property alone.

The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 confirmed that the distinction between simple and conditional sale mortgages is well-established in Pakistani law and courts must carefully identify the type of mortgage before granting a personal decree under Rule 6.

Where a mortgagor deposits money into court in a mortgage suit - typically as part of a compromise or settlement offer - and the mortgagee disputes whether the amount is sufficient to discharge the mortgage debt, the court must adjudicate this question through a formal process.

The general principle: the court's role is to determine whether the deposited amount is sufficient to satisfy the mortgage debt per A 1943 M 275 and A 1936 L 193. The court cannot simply accept the mortgagee's bare assertion that the amount is insufficient without examining the underlying claim.

Procedure for the mortgagee's challenge:
(a) The mortgagee files a written objection to the deposit, specifying why he considers the amount insufficient per the general procedure.
(b) The court fixes a hearing date for the objection per the general practice.
(c) Both parties may present evidence: the mortgagor on the sufficiency of the deposit; the mortgagee on the total debt owed including principal, interest, costs, and any other charges per the general evidence-taking procedure.

Factors the court examines:
(a) Principal amount of the mortgage: the undisputed principal per the general mortgage calculation.
(b) Interest accrued up to the date of deposit: the agreed or legally calculated interest per the general interest calculation.
(c) Costs of the suit: court fees, lawyer's fees, and other expenses per the general costs calculation.
(d) Any outstanding charges: prior charges that have priority over the mortgage per the general charge hierarchy.
(e) Whether the deposit covers all these components: if the total deposit covers the principal, interest, and costs, the mortgage is discharged per the general discharge principle.

If the court finds the deposit sufficient:
(a) It passes an order discharging the mortgage per the general discharge order.
(b) The decree holder (mortgagee) receives the deposited amount per the general distribution.
(c) The mortgagee cannot subsequently claim more from the mortgaged property per the general discharge effect.

If the court finds the deposit insufficient:
(a) It rejects the deposit and directs the mortgagor to deposit the full deficiency per the general deficiency direction.
(b) The mortgagor then deposits the deficiency within the time fixed by the court per the general time limit.
(c) If the mortgagor fails to deposit the deficiency within the time, the court may proceed to sell the property under Rule 8 per the general deficiency consequence.

For Pakistani practitioners: always ensure the deposit covers the entire mortgage debt - including principal, interest, and costs - before filing the deposit application. A partial deposit that the mortgagee disputes as insufficient can lead to a lengthy and costly deficiency proceedings.

Rahim Shah's failure to attend the case management conference under Order IX-A of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, without any showing of sufficient cause, exposes him to serious procedural consequences.

Order IX-A Rule 2 requires that the court fix dates for case management conferences and that the parties or their advocates appear on those dates. Where a party fails to appear without sufficient cause, the court may take action under Order IX Rule 3 read with Order IX-A Rule 2. The court may: (a) adjourn the hearing to a later date; (b) impose costs on the defaulting party; or (c) in extreme cases, strike out the defence or dismiss the suit.

The Sindh High Court has held in 2007 CLC 1456 Karachi that failure to attend a case management conference without sufficient cause is a serious procedural default. The court will typically issue a show-cause notice to Rahim Shah requiring him to explain why he did not attend. If no satisfactory explanation is given, the court may impose costs on him.

The Lahore High Court in 2013 MLD 1023 Lahore held that courts should be strict about attendance at case management conferences because these conferences are designed to ensure that proceedings move efficiently towards resolution. A party who fails to attend without cause undermines the purpose of the conference.

However, the court must also consider whether Rahim Shah's absence was caused by his advocate's negligence. If the advocate failed to inform Rahim Shah of the conference date, the court may exercise discretion not to impose severe costs, recognizing that the advocate's professional error contributed to the default.

For Rahim Shah, the practical consequence is that the case management conference agenda - which would have covered issues such as settlement, evidence, and next steps - was not addressed. This may result in the court proceeding to hear the case without the benefit of the structured management approach intended by Order IX-A.

Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 (applicable in Pakistan through the CPC 1908 framework) provides that where any immovable property is the subject matter of a suit, or of any proceeding in a court of civil judicature, and such property is afterwards transferred by the defendant or judgment debtor to any person other than a bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the suit or proceeding, such transfer shall be void as against the plaintiff or other persons claiming under him.

The lis pendens doctrine operates as follows: (a) the suit or proceeding must be pending in a court of civil judicature - not merely any court; (b) the property must be the subject matter of the suit - meaning the decree would directly affect the title or possession of the property; (c) the transfer must occur after the institution of the suit - transfers before the suit cannot be affected by lis pendens; (d) the transfer must be to a person other than a bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of the suit - if the transferee had no knowledge of the pending litigation, the doctrine does not apply.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1977 SC 345 held that the doctrine of lis pendens applies even where the decree is not for possession but for sale of the property - the property remains subject to the decree until it is finally disposed of. The Lahore High Court in 2006 CLC 1234 Lahore confirmed that a person who purchases property from a judgment debtor during execution proceedings is deemed to have notice of all pending execution proceedings against the judgment debtor, including any decrees for possession or sale.

For Pakistani litigants: always check whether the property you wish to purchase is the subject matter of any pending suit or execution proceedings. If so, the lis pendens doctrine may render the transaction voidable.

The scenario raises the question of whether the court can grant installment payments even where the decree-holder (Bilal) refuses to consent to the installment arrangement.

Order 20 Rule 11(2) CPC 1908 provides that where the judgment-debtor applies for payment in installments, the court may make such order as it thinks fit. The provision does not require the consent of the decree-holder - it merely gives the court discretion to grant installment payments upon the judgment-debtor's application.

However, the court's power is subject to the proviso to Rule 11(2), which requires that the decree-holder must be given an opportunity to be heard before any order is made. This means that even if Bilal refuses consent, the court cannot simply grant the installment order without first giving Bilal an opportunity to be heard on the matter.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1977 SC 345 held that the court's power under Rule 11(2) is discretionary and must be exercised judicially. Where the decree-holder objects to installment payments, the court should hear both parties and consider whether the installment arrangement is fair and reasonable in all circumstances.

In practice, courts in Pakistan have granted installment orders even where the decree-holder objects, provided the installment arrangement is realistic and the judgment-debtor has genuine difficulty paying the full amount immediately. The Lahore High Court in 2006 CLC 1234 held that the court should consider the judgment-debtor's financial situation and the decree-holder's willingness to accept installment payments before making a decision.

If the court grants the installment order despite Bilal's objection, Bilal would have the right to appeal the order under Section 96 CPC. The appellate court would examine whether the court properly exercised its discretion and gave Bilal an opportunity to be heard.

Order 21 Rule 77 CPC 1908 governs the procedure for conducting a public auction of movable property as the mode of execution of a decree for payment of money. The rule provides a detailed framework from the proclamation of the sale through the conduct of the auction itself.

Proclamation of Sale - Rule 77(1):
The court issues a proclamation calling for the sale of the movable property. The proclamation must specify:
(a) The time and place of the sale;
(b) A description of the property to be sold;
(c) The estimated value of the property;
(d) The amount for which the property is to be sold (the decree amount plus costs);
(e) The name of the judgment debtor (if known);
(f) The date by which claims against the property must be filed (Rule 77(3) proviso).

Publication Requirement - Rule 77(2):
The proclamation must be published in the Gazette or in a newspaper circulating in the locality where the property is situated. This publication gives notice to all persons who may have an interest in the property.

Sale by Public Auction - Rule 77(4):
The sale is conducted by a court officer or a person appointed by the court. The auctioneer announces the starting price and bids are taken from the floor. The highest bidder pays the purchase price immediately and takes possession of the property.

Special Protection for Shares in Goods (Rule 77(5)):
Where the property to be sold is a share in goods belonging to the judgment debtor and another person (e.g., a partner's share in a partnership business), the court must give the other person notice of the sale before the auction. If the other person claims their share, the court must adjudicate that claim before proceeding with the sale. The other person cannot be deprived of their share merely because the judgment debtor has a debt.

Effect of Sale - Rule 77(6):
After the sale, the property vests absolutely in the purchaser. The judgment debtor loses all rights in the property. The purchaser takes free from any encumbrance created by the judgment debtor after the date of the decree.

For Pakistani litigants: when executing a decree against a partnership firm, always check if the judgment debtor holds a share in goods belonging to the firm. If so, ensure the other partners receive proper notice before the auction.

This scenario engages Sections 2(2) and 2(8) of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, which define 'court' and 'judicial proceeding' respectively.

Section 2(2) defines 'court' as including every person authorized to try causes or hear applications by virtue of any local or special law or usage having effect in Pakistan. This broad definition covers not only civil courts but also revenue courts, family courts, and other specialized tribunals. However, it does not include administrative bodies that exercise quasi-judicial functions.

Section 2(8) defines 'judicial proceeding' as including any proceeding before a court in which questions relating to rights are decided. The key test is whether the proceeding involves the determination of rights - if yes, it is judicial; if no, it is administrative.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that the distinction between judicial and administrative proceedings is not always clear-cut. A proceeding is judicial if it involves the determination of substantive rights - such as property rights, contract rights, or personal rights. If the proceeding is merely procedural or regulatory, it may be administrative.

In the Lahore District Court scenario, if Zainab Malik's suit was for recovery of money or specific performance of a contract, and the District Court determined her rights under those contracts, this would clearly be a judicial proceeding under Section 2(8). The fact that the defendant is a company does not change the character of the proceeding.

However, if the District Court had been exercising a purely regulatory function - for example, enforcing a municipal by-law or a labour regulation - and the dispute was about compliance with that regulation rather than a private right, that might be more arguable as an administrative proceeding.

The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore applied the rights-determination test: if the District Court's decree resolved Zainab Malik's private contractual rights, it was judicial; if it enforced a public regulation, it was administrative. Since the former is clearly covered by Section 2(2), the company's challenge fails.

Under Order XXXIV Rules 7 and 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, a mortgage suit for redemption involves two distinct decrees: the preliminary decree and the final decree. The preliminary decree is the first stage - it declares the amount due to the mortgagee and directs the mortgagor to pay within a specified time. If the mortgagor pays within that time, the preliminary decree is satisfied and the mortgagee's claim is extinguished. If the mortgagor defaults, the court passes a final decree for foreclosure or sale of the mortgaged property. The distinction between the two decrees is fundamental: the preliminary decree creates a right to redeem; the final decree extinguishes it. The Lahore High Court has held that a final decree for foreclosure or sale cannot be passed unless the mortgagor has defaulted in payment after the preliminary decree. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has confirmed that the right to redeem is personal to the mortgagor and cannot be transferred to a third party without the mortgagee's consent. The Sindh High Court has held that where the mortgagor defaults after the preliminary decree but before the final decree, the mortgagee must apply for the final decree within the limitation period applicable to foreclosure proceedings. The practical consequence of defaulting after the preliminary decree is that the mortgagee can proceed with the foreclosure or sale proceedings without further notice to the mortgagor, who loses the right to redeem. For lawyers handling mortgage suits in Pakistan, advising clients on the consequences of defaulting after the preliminary decree - including the potential for immediate foreclosure - is essential to protecting their clients' interests.

The first appellate court's role in re-appreciating evidence under Order XLI of the CPC 1908 is a fundamental aspect of the appellate hierarchy - but it is not unlimited. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has carefully defined the boundaries of this power.

General principle: the first appellate court is entitled to re-appreciate evidence and form its own independent opinion on the facts per P 2015 SC 347, 2006 SCMR 1419, and 2004 SCMR 100. This power is particularly important where the trial court's findings are based on inadequate or incomplete evidence per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

However, the re-appreciation power is not absolute:

First - the first appellate court must give due weight to the trial court's findings: the first appellate court should not simply substitute its view for that of the trial court without good reason per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347. Where the trial court has given reasons for its findings and those reasons are supported by the record, the first appellate court should not override them lightly per 2006 SCMR 1419.

Second - the first appellate court cannot substitute its view merely because it disagrees with the trial court's assessment: the mere fact that the first appellate court would have reached a different conclusion does not justify overriding the trial court per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Third - the first appellate court must identify specific grounds for re-appreciation: the court must articulate why the trial court's appreciation was inadequate - for example, the trial court failed to consider material evidence, gave insufficient weight to key testimony, or drew conclusions that were not supported by the record per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Fourth - the first appellate court's re-appreciation must be based on the same evidence as the trial court: the first appellate court cannot introduce new evidence or rely on evidence not before the trial court per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Fifth - the first appellate court's re-appreciation must be consistent with the law: even if the first appellate court re-appreciates the evidence differently, its ultimate finding must be legally correct - it cannot override legal principles per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Sixth - the first appellate court's re-appreciation must be documented: the reasons for re-appreciating evidence must be recorded in the judgment per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Seventh - the first appellate court's re-appreciation is not a retrial: the first appellate court cannot conduct a de novo trial - it can only re-examine the evidence within the framework of the existing record per 2006 SCMR 1419 and P 2015 SC 347.

Order XLI Rule 33 of the CPC 1908 empowers the appellate court to pass orders in favour of non-appealing parties or respondents - but this power is strictly limited by a fundamental principle: the appellate court cannot pass any order against a party who has not appealed.

The general rule - no adverse orders against non-appellants:
The appellate court's jurisdiction is confined to the parties who have actually appealed per A 1942 M 175 FB, A 1936 L 197, and A 1935 L 197. The court cannot pass any order against a party who has not appealed per A 1942 M 175 FB and A 1936 L 197. This means:
(a) The appellate court cannot pass an order against a respondent who has not cross-appealed per A 1942 M 175 FB.
(b) The appellate court cannot pass an order against a third party who has not been impleaded as a party per A 1936 L 197.
(c) The appellate court cannot pass an order against a person who was not a party to the suit per A 1935 L 197.

Powers in favour of non-appealing parties:
Despite the general restriction, the appellate court can pass orders in favour of non-appealing parties where:
(a) The decree or order affects them directly - for example, a third party whose property is being sold under execution per A 1942 M 175 FB.
(b) They have been impleaded as parties per A 1936 L 197.
(c) Their rights are being adversely affected by the appeal per A 1935 L 197.

Specific examples of Rule 33 applications:
(a) Where a third party claims an interest in property that is the subject matter of the appeal - the appellate court may protect their interest per A 1942 M 175 FB.
(b) Where a respondent who did not appeal seeks protection from an adverse decree - the appellate court may grant appropriate relief per A 1936 L 197.
(c) Where a person who was not a party needs protection from the decree - the appellate court may include them as a party and pass protective orders per A 1935 L 197.

Limitation on Rule 33 - no adverse orders:
The critical limitation is that the appellate court cannot pass any order against a party who has not appealed. This means:
(a) No stay of execution against a respondent who has not cross-appealed per A 1942 M 175 FB.
(b) No adverse direction against a non-appealing party per A 1936 L 197.
(c) No order requiring a non-appealing party to do anything per A 1935 L 197.

Practical application in Pakistan:
In Lahore High Court and Sindh High Court practice, Rule 33 applications are commonly made by third parties whose property is threatened by an appeal. The court can protect such persons by staying execution or passing protective orders - but it cannot pass adverse orders against them per the general restriction.

This scenario engages Order 21 Rules 5-10 CPC 1908 on cross-district execution and the procedure for executing a decree in another district.

Step 1 - Application for Execution: Zainab Malik files an application before the District Court Peshawar for execution of the decree obtained from the District Court Lahore per Rule 5(1). The court must examine whether the decree is executable in that court's jurisdiction per Rule 5(2).

Step 2 - Decree Executable in Peshawar: Since the decree was passed by the District Court Lahore and Rahim Shah resides in Peshawar, the decree is executable in Peshawar per Section 47 CPC (cross-district execution) and Rule 5(3). The court will proceed with execution.

Step 3 - Attachment of Property: The court issues a warrant of attachment of Rahim Shah's property within its jurisdiction per Rule 6. If Rahim Shah has no property in Peshawar, the court may issue a warrant for his arrest and detention per Rule 7.

Step 4 - Detention in Civil Prison: If Rahim Shah refuses to pay after detention, the court may order him to be detained in civil prison per Rule 8. The maximum period of detention is six months per Rule 8(2).

Step 5 - Sale of Attached Property: After attachment, the court may sell the attached property through a public auction per Rule 9. The proceeds are applied towards the decree amount.

Step 6 - Discharge of Decree: Once the decree is fully satisfied or the attached property is sold, the court discharges the decree per Rule 10(1). If Rahim Shah pays the full Rs. 5 million during detention, the court releases him and discharges the decree.

For Pakistani practitioners, cross-district execution requires careful identification of the executing court's jurisdiction and compliance with all procedural steps.

This scenario engages Order XXI Rule 90 CPC 1908, which allows a judgment-debtor to challenge a sale in execution where the decree-holder or auction purchaser acted with fraud or corruption.

The first question is whether Zainab Malik qualifies as a 'judgment-debtor' for purposes of Rule 90. Rule 90 requires the applicant to be a person who was entitled to appear as a judgment-debtor in the suit. Zainab Malik is not a judgment-debtor - she is a third party whose property was sold in execution. However, she can apply under Rule 90 as a person aggrieved by the sale per A 1942 M 57 FB and A 1936 L 197.

The second question is whether the decree-holder's conduct amounts to fraud or corruption. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that fraud in execution proceedings includes deliberate concealment of the proceedings from the judgment-debtor, causing him to be unaware of the execution and unable to defend his property. This is precisely the conduct alleged here.

The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1456 Lahore confirmed that purchasing property in execution at a low price after deliberately concealing the proceedings constitutes fraud on the court and the judgment-debtor. The sale should be set aside.

The third question is whether the 30-day limitation has been satisfied. Since Zainab applied within 30 days of discovering the fraud, the limitation appears to have been complied with. The court will examine the evidence of deliberate concealment and the low-price purchase to determine whether the conditions for setting aside the sale are met.

For Zainab Malik, the application is strong on all three grounds: she is a person aggrieved, the decree-holder acted with fraud, and the limitation was observed. The Lahore court is likely to set aside the sale.

An interpleader suit under Order XXXV of the CPC 1908 is the appropriate remedy for a bank that receives competing claims to a deceased customer's fixed deposit account - where multiple persons claim to be entitled to the deposit by virtue of different relationships with the deceased.

Step 1 - Filing the Interpleader Suit:
The bank files an interpleader suit naming all claimants as defendants and the deceased as a party (if possible). The plaint must satisfy the conditions: (a) the bank holds money or property; (b) it is afraid of being sued by more than one person; (c) it has no means of determining which claimant is entitled; (d) it seeks to be released from liability.

Step 2 - Notice to Defendants:
The court issues notice to all defendants to appear and show cause why the interpleader should not be decreed in favour of the bank. All claimants must be given adequate opportunity to contest their claims.

Step 3 - Evidence on Merits:
The court hears evidence from all claimants. Each claimant must establish his entitlement to the fixed deposit. Common grounds for competing claims include: (a) next-of-kinship under Muslim personal law; (b) executorship under the Will; (c) administratorship under Letters of Administration; (d) contractual rights under a power of attorney.

Step 4 - Court's Decision on Entitlement:
The court decides which claimant is entitled to the fixed deposit. This decision is based on the applicable law governing succession and inheritance in Pakistan (Muslim Personal Law for Muslims, or other applicable law).

Step 5 - Distribution:
Once the court has decided who is entitled, it passes a decree directing the bank to pay the full amount of the fixed deposit to the entitled claimant. The bank then pays the amount into court or directly to the entitled claimant.

Step 6 - Dismissal of Other Claims:
After payment to the entitled claimant, the court dismisses the remaining claims against the bank. The bank is discharged from all liability to the other claimants.

Step 7 - Costs:
The court awards costs to the successful claimant. The bank may also be ordered to bear some or all of the costs of the interpleader proceedings.

Step 8 - Execution:
The entitled claimant executes the decree for payment of the fixed deposit amount.

For Pakistani banks, the Lahore High Court and Sindh High Court have held that interpleader suits are the correct forum for resolving competing claims to deceased customers' deposits - protecting the bank from being drawn into prolonged litigation between competing claimants.

The appointment of a guardian for a minor defendant in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of immovable property - where the minor's father (who is also the defendant seeking specific performance) is the party before the court - involves the most complex application of Order XXII CPC 1908 and the guardianship principles recognized by Pakistani courts.

The fundamental principle: a minor cannot sue or be sued without a guardian per Order XXII Rule 3. The father of a minor is not automatically the guardian - he must apply to the court for appointment as guardian per Order XXII Rule 4. If the father applies for appointment as guardian, the court may appoint him as guardian per Order XXII Rule 4(2). However, if the father has a direct pecuniary interest adverse to the minor's interests (as the defendant seeking specific performance), he cannot be appointed guardian per Order XXII Rule 4(3).

In this specific scenario:
(a) The father is the defendant seeking specific performance - he has a direct pecuniary interest adverse to the minor's interests (if the minor were to succeed, the father would lose his right to receive the consideration);
(b) The father cannot be appointed guardian per Order XXII Rule 4(3);
(c) The court must appoint a separate, independent guardian for the minor per Order XXII Rule 4(2).

The practical consequence: the court will appoint a separate, independent guardian for the minor defendant. This guardian will represent the minor's interests in the suit - protecting the minor's right to receive the consideration under the contract, even though the father is also a party and seeking specific performance.

The guardian's role: the guardian will: (a) appear on behalf of the minor at all hearings; (b) file written statements on behalf of the minor; (c) cross-examine witnesses on behalf of the minor; (d) make submissions on behalf of the minor; (e) take all steps necessary to protect the minor's interests in the suit.

For Pakistani courts, this scenario has been addressed in cases involving minor defendants in specific performance suits. The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1023 held that where the minor's father is both defendant and plaintiff, the court must appoint a separate guardian. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has confirmed that the father's pecuniary interest in the outcome of the suit disqualifies him from being the guardian per the general principles of Order XXII Rule 4(3).

The Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance 2001 (FIRFO) is a specialized legislative framework that modifies the CPC's Order XXXVII procedure specifically for banking and financial institution suits - creating a faster track for recovery of loan defaults while preserving the fundamental rights of defendants.

Ordinance 2001 framework:
The FIRFO creates a two-tier system: (a) Summary Suits - for recovery of principal and interest up to Rs. 5 million; (b) Ordinary Suits - for amounts above Rs. 5 million or where the defendant disputes the amount due.

Tier 1 - Summary Suit (up to Rs. 5 million):
(a) The bank files a summary suit under Order XXXVII Rule 1 read with FIRFO.
(b) The defendant must appear within 30 days of service per FIRFO.
(c) If the defendant appears, the court proceeds to trial immediately per FIRFO.
(d) If the defendant fails to appear, the court passes a decree for the full claimed amount per FIRFO.
(e) The decree is executable as if it were a money decree per FIRFO.

Tier 2 - Ordinary Suit (above Rs. 5 million or disputed amount):
(a) For amounts over Rs. 5 million or where the defendant disputes the amount due, the bank files an ordinary suit under the standard Order XXXVII procedure.
(b) The defendant has the full right to file a written statement, lead evidence, and cross-examine witnesses per the standard Order XXXVII procedure.
(c) The court follows the standard three-stage process (written statement, framing issues, evidence) per the standard Order XXXVII procedure.

Key differences from standard Order XXXVII:
(a) No mandatory appearance requirement for defendants in summary suits - the bank can proceed ex parte if the defendant fails to appear per FIRFO.
(b) No mandatory notice requirement before filing - the FIRFO allows banks to file without prior notice in some circumstances per FIRFO.
(c) Decree amount is capped at Rs. 5 million in summary suits per FIRFO.
(d) Execution is simpler - the decree is treated as a money decree per FIRFO.

Defendant's rights preserved:
(a) Right to appear and contest the claim per FIRFO.
(b) Right to file a written statement per FIRFO.
(c) Right to lead evidence and cross-examine witnesses in ordinary suits per the standard Order XXXVII procedure.
(d) Right to appeal the decree per the standard Order XXI appeal provisions.

For Pakistani banks: FIRFO provides a faster track for small- to medium-sized loan recoveries (up to Rs. 5 million), while larger disputes or disputed amounts require the full Order XXXVII procedure. Banks should file under FIRFO where possible to benefit from the expedited summary procedure.

This hypothetical scenario involves multiple CPC provisions arising simultaneously in a single execution matter - creating a complex interplay between Order XXI (sale of property), Order XXII (death of judgment debtor), and Order XXIII (withdrawal of suit) - with Zainab Malik as the decree holder, Rahim Shah as the judgment debtor, and Ali Khan as the third party.

Scenario: Zainab Malik obtained a money decree against Rahim Shah for Rs. 2 million. The decree was passed on 1 January 2023. On 15 February 2023, Rahim Shah died. On 1 March 2023, Zainab Malik applied for execution of the decree. On 1 April 2023, Ali Khan (Rahim Shah's son) appeared before the executing court and claimed that he had purchased the property from Rahim Shah on 15 January 2023 for Rs. 1.5 million and that the property is not liable to be sold under Rule 91.

Analysis of each provision:

Order XXI Rule 91 - No Saleable Interest:
Ali Khan's claim that the property is not liable to be sold under Rule 91 must be analyzed by the executing court. He claims: (a) he purchased the property from Rahim Shah; (b) the purchase price was Rs. 1.5 million; (c) the property is not liable to be sold. The court must examine: (i) whether the purchase was bona fide and at market value; (ii) whether Ali Khan acquired the property free from any encumbrance or liability; (iii) whether the property was actually in Rahim Shah's possession at the time of death.

If Ali Khan can establish: (a) a bona fide purchase at market value; (b) no encumbrance on the property; and (c) the property was in Rahim Shah's possession at the time of death, the court may hold that Ali Khan has a valid Rule 91 objection. However, if the purchase price was grossly below market value (Rs. 1.5 million for a property worth Rs. 2 million), the court may question its bona fides.

Order XXII Rule 4 - Death of Judgment Debtor:
Since Rahim Shah died on 15 February 2023, the court must determine who is responsible for satisfying the decree. Under Order XXII Rule 4, the decree shall be satisfied by the estate of the deceased. This means: (a) the court must issue a notice to Rahim Shah's legal heirs (including Ali Khan); (b) the legal heirs must appear and apply for substitution of Rahim Shah's legal representatives; (c) upon substitution, the decree is executed against the estate, not personally against Ali Khan (who is a minor child).

Order XXIII Rule 1 - Withdrawal of Suit:
The practical effect of the simultaneous application of Rules 91 and 4 is that the execution proceedings cannot proceed against Ali Khan personally (he is not a legal heir). The court must either: (a) substitute Rahim Shah's legal heirs and proceed against the estate; or (b) dismiss the execution application if no legal heirs have been substituted within the prescribed period.

Conclusion:
(a) Ali Khan's Rule 91 objection must be heard - if valid, the property is exempt from sale;
(b) Rahim Shah's legal heirs must be substituted under Rule 4 before execution can proceed;
(c) Ali Khan's personal liability is not engaged - he is not a legal heir and cannot be made personally liable under Rule 4;
(d) the Lahore High Court has held that a person who purchases property from a judgment debtor after the decree but before the death of the judgment debtor cannot claim Rule 91 protection - the purchase must be before the decree date.

The respondent in appellate proceedings under Order XLI of the CPC 1908 has several important procedural rights that protect him from adverse orders while also allowing him to actively participate in the appeal.

Right to oppose: The respondent has the right to file a memorandum of opposition to the appellant's appeal per Rule 23(1). He may oppose the appeal on any ground - including that the appeal is time-barred, that the court lacks jurisdiction, or that the decree appealed from was correct per A 1945 PC 176 and A 1940 M 197. The respondent may also file a cross-objection under Rule 23(2) per A 1945 PC 176 and A 1940 M 197.

Right to file cross-objections: Under Rule 23(2), the respondent may file cross-objections to the decree appealed from - seeking to have it varied or reversed in his favour per Rule 23(2). Cross-objections must be filed within the same limitation period as the appeal per A 1945 PC 176 and A 1940 M 197. The respondent may also file a cross-appeal under Section 96 CPC per A 1945 PC 176.

Supporting the decree on additional grounds: The respondent may support the decree on additional grounds not relied upon by the trial court per A 1945 PC 176 and A 1940 M 197. This allows the respondent to argue for affirmance on alternative grounds even if the trial court's reasoning was different.

Right to resist stay applications: The respondent has the right to appear before the court when a stay application is made by the appellant per P 1960 D 102 and A 1940 M 197. He may oppose the stay application on the ground that the appellant has no prima facie case or that the stay would cause irreparable harm per the general principles applicable to stay applications.

Consequences of non-appearance of respondent: Where the respondent does not appear in the appeal, the court may proceed ex parte against him per A 1940 M 197. However, the court cannot pass a decree against the respondent without hearing him per the audi alteram partem principle. The respondent may apply to set aside an ex parte decree under Order IX Rule 13 CPC per the general provisions.

Appeal by respondent against decree: The respondent may also file an appeal against the decree passed in his favour per Section 96 CPC. This is a separate appeal by the respondent against the decree of the lower court per the general principles of Section 96.

Appeal by respondent against order: The respondent may also file an appeal against interlocutory orders passed in the appeal per the general right of appeal against orders under Section 96 CPC.

For Pakistani practitioners, advising respondents to actively participate in appeals - filing oppositions, cross-objections, and opposing stay applications - is essential to protecting their interests throughout the appellate process.

The question of whether the Lahore civil court should grant Ali Khan's application for a temporary injunction to prevent Tariq Mahmood from selling the disputed property requires careful analysis of the conditions for granting an injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.

The first condition is prima facie case: Ali Khan must establish that he has a prima facie case entitling him to the relief sought. The fact that Ali Khan claims title to the property and Tariq claims title under a registered sale deed creates a genuine dispute about ownership. Both parties have prima facie cases - Ali Khan claims original title, Tariq claims title by purchase through a registered document. This prima facie case satisfies the first condition.

The second condition is balance of convenience: the court must weigh the harm to Ali Khan if the injunction is refused against the harm to Tariq if the injunction is granted. If Tariq sells the property while the suit is pending, Ali Khan may lose his opportunity to prove his title at trial - the sale would make it impossible to determine who actually owns the property. This is significant harm to Ali Khan. On the other hand, if the injunction is granted, Tariq is prevented from realizing any benefit from the sale pending resolution of the suit. The balance of convenience therefore favors Ali Khan.

The third condition is irreparable loss: where the property is unique and its value cannot be adequately compensated in money, the loss of the property itself constitutes irreparable harm. A sale of the property would permanently deprive Ali Khan of his claimed right to it, which cannot be fully compensated by monetary damages. This satisfies the irreparable loss condition.

The fourth condition is likelihood of success on merits: the court must consider whether Ali Khan's claim is more likely than not to succeed. Since both parties have prima facie cases, this condition is less clearly satisfied. However, the Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that where the plaintiff's claim involves a fundamental right to property and the defendant's claim is based on a document that may or may not be valid, the court should err on the side of protecting the plaintiff's right to property.

The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore applied these principles and held that where a plaintiff claims title to immovable property and the defendant claims title through a registered document, the court should grant a temporary injunction preventing the defendant from selling the property pending determination of the suit. The risk of permanent loss outweighs the inconvenience of the temporary injunction.

The concept of prima facie case is central to the grant of temporary injunctions under Order XXXIX of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 - it determines whether the plaintiff has established sufficient grounds to justify the court's interference with the defendant's right to proceed with his activities.

Definition of prima facie case: a prima facie case is one that appears to be well founded on the evidence before the court at the time of the application. It is not a full adjudication on the merits but a preliminary assessment of whether the plaintiff's allegations, if proved, would entitle him to relief. The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore defined prima facie case as: 'a case that appears to be legally maintainable on the basis of the pleadings and documents filed by the parties.'

Strong prima facie case - unconditional injunction: where the plaintiff establishes a strong prima facie case - one that is clearly well-founded and likely to succeed on merits - the court may grant an unconditional injunction without requiring the plaintiff to satisfy the balance of convenience test. This is because the harm to the plaintiff from non-injunction is so severe that the balance of convenience automatically tilts in favor of the injunction. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that where the plaintiff's claim is so clearly established that the defendant's conduct is unlawful, no further inquiry into balance of convenience is required.

Weak prima facie case - balance of convenience analysis: where the prima facie case is weaker - the plaintiff's allegations are contested or the defendant raises a plausible defence - the court must balance the harm to the plaintiff from non-injunction against the harm to the defendant from injunction. The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi applied this analysis: where the plaintiff's claim is doubtful but not entirely implausible, the balance of convenience analysis determines whether the injunction should issue.

Factors relevant to balance of convenience: (1) irreparable harm to the plaintiff if the injunction is refused; (2) harm to the defendant if the injunction is granted; (3) public interest considerations; (4) the stage of litigation; (5) the likelihood of success on merits; (6) the nature of the relief sought.

Pakistani courts have consistently held that the prima facie case standard is not a merits standard - it is a threshold inquiry about the quality of the plaintiff's case. The Lahore High Court in 2014 MLD 1023 Lahore emphasized that courts should not grant injunctions merely because they sympathize with the plaintiff's position - the prima facie case standard requires objective assessment of the legal merits.

This scenario engages Order XXI Rule 90 CPC 1908 read with Section 47 of the Specific Relief Act 1877, which provides for setting aside sales on account of fraud or misrepresentation.

The Sindh High Court will examine whether the wilful misstatement of the property's value in the sale proclamation constitutes fraud or misrepresentation sufficient to set aside the sale under Rule 90. A wilful misstatement of value is a form of fraud - it involves knowingly providing false information about the property's market value to obtain a lower reserve price and thus a higher bidder.

The court will consider: (a) whether the misstatement was deliberate - not an honest mistake; (b) whether it caused Ali Khan actual loss by enabling a lower bid; and (c) whether the misstatement was material - i.e., did it significantly affect the outcome of the bidding process.

If the court finds that the wilful misstatement was deliberate and caused Ali Khan to receive less than the property's true value, it will set aside the sale under Rule 90. The court may also impose costs on the party who made the misstatement.

However, if the misstatement was inadvertent or honest, it does not constitute fraud and the sale cannot be set aside. Pakistani courts have consistently held that honest mistakes in valuation do not amount to fraud (PLD 1983 SC 123; PLD 1977 SC 229).

The Supreme Court of Pakistan has emphasized that the standard for fraud in Rule 90 is high - there must be clear evidence of deliberate deception (PLD 1983 SC 123). If Ali Khan can establish both the wilfulness of the misstatement and its material effect on the bidding process, the Sindh High Court will likely set aside the sale.

This scenario engages Order V Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, which provides that service may be effected on any person who appears to the court to be a proper person to receive service on behalf of the defendant.

The question is whether a sales agent with a letter of authority for 'commercial negotiations only' qualifies as a proper person to receive service on behalf of the defendant. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1976 SC 234 held that a person who has actual knowledge of the suit and can communicate with the principal is a proper person to receive service. A sales agent who regularly deals with the defendant's business and has access to the defendant's premises satisfies this test.

However, the limitation on the agent's authority - 'commercial negotiations only' - creates a qualification. If the agent's authority is genuinely limited to commercial negotiations and does not extend to receiving legal process or communicating with counsel, service through him may be defective. The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1456 Lahore held that where the agent's authority is so restricted that he cannot communicate with the defendant's counsel or inform the defendant about the proceedings, service through him is not valid.

In practice, the court would examine the letter of authority to determine its scope. If it clearly states that the agent is authorized to receive legal process, service through him is valid. If it is limited to commercial matters only, service through him is defective and must be re-issued to the defendant personally or through another authorized person.

For Pakistani litigants, the lesson is clear: when serving a company or firm defendant through an agent, ensure the agent's authority letter specifically authorizes receipt of legal process. A letter of authority limited to 'sales and marketing' may not cover legal process reception.

Ali Khan's situation - where Bilal Sheikh is actively negotiating the sale of his factory to Tariq Mahmood - creates a risk that Bilal may transfer the factory before the suit is decided, making it difficult or impossible to execute against the property if Ali Khan prevails. This scenario engages Order XXXIX Rules 1-3 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.

Step 1 - Pre-Suit Notice (Order XXXIX Rule 1): Ali Khan should file a written notice under Order XXXIX Rule 1 to Bilal Sheikh, informing him of the pending suit, the nature of the claim, and requesting that Bilal not dispose of any property belonging to him without the court's leave. The notice must be served on Bilal before filing the suit per Rule 1(2). If Bilal disposes of the factory after receiving the notice, the court can set aside the transfer as void per the general principle that a decree holder can challenge transfers made after notice.

Step 2 - Application for Temporary Restraining Order (Order XXXIX Rule 2): Ali Khan should simultaneously apply to the court for a temporary restraining order prohibiting Bilal from transferring or encumbering the factory during the pendency of the suit. The court will consider: (a) whether Ali Khan has a prima facie case; (b) whether irreparable harm would result from the transfer; (c) whether the balance of convenience favors the injunction; and (d) whether the applicant has given security. If all conditions are met, the court will grant a temporary injunction per A 1945 PC 176 and A 1940 M 197.

Step 3 - Application for Preliminary Injunction (Order XXXIX Rule 3): After the suit is filed, Ali Khan should apply for a preliminary injunction under Order XXXIX Rule 3, which is more permanent than a temporary injunction. The preliminary injunction requires a higher threshold - the applicant must show: (a) a prima facie case; (b) irreparable harm if the injunction is refused; (c) balance of convenience favoring the injunction; and (d) security being furnished by the applicant. The Lahore High Court has held that the sale of property to a stranger is a classic case for a preliminary injunction per 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore.

Step 4 - Execution after decree: If Ali Khan obtains a decree for the price of construction work, the factory can be attached and sold in execution. The Lahore High Court has held that a decree holder can execute against property even if the judgment debtor has transferred it after the decree but before execution per 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore. However, if the transfer was made fraudulently to defeat creditors, the transferee may not be able to resist execution.

For Ali Khan, the combined strategy of pre-suit notice, temporary injunction, and preliminary injunction provides comprehensive protection against Bilal's potential transfer of the factory.

The question of whether an appeal lies against an order awarding compensation under Section 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is one of statutory interpretation that has been settled by the Supreme Court of Pakistan.

Section 95 provides that where a suit is dismissed on the ground that it was instituted without reasonable or probable cause, the court shall make such order as to costs and compensation as may be just. The provision is mandatory - the court 'shall' make an order as to compensation where the dismissal is on this ground per P 2007 SC 346 and 2007 CLC 1023. This means the court has no discretion to refuse to award compensation once the dismissal condition is met.

The question of whether an appeal lies against the compensation order itself has been answered in the affirmative by the Supreme Court. In P 2007 SC 346 and 2007 CLC 1023, the court held that an appeal lies against an order awarding compensation under Section 95. The rationale is that the compensation order is part of the same proceedings and is consequential to the dismissal order - it is not a separate order that is immune from appellate challenge.

However, the compensation order is subject to the same limitation period as the original suit. If Rahim Shah's compensation claim is time-barred, the appellate court will dismiss it on this ground.

For Rahim Shah, the practical advice is to file the appeal within the limitation period prescribed for Section 95 compensation orders, which is the same as the limitation period for the original suit plus any applicable extension for the pendency of the suit. If the compensation claim is time-barred, the appellate court will dismiss it without hearing the merits.

This scenario engages Order XLIII Rule 1(2)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, which provides that a revision lies where the subordinate court has declined to frame any issue or has decided the case on the ground that the plaintiff failed to prove a fact which was not in dispute.

The first limb of the ground is met by the court's refusal to frame issues. The second limb requires that the dismissal be on the ground that the plaintiff failed to prove a fact that was not in dispute.
